prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map captures the 3D layout of a raised construction floor sloping away from the camera wearer toward a recessed interior background (2.5 to 4.0 m away, dark) in frames 1 to 3, and a vertical concrete pillar (1.0 to 1.5 m away, medium-bright) separating the ledge from a lower exterior ground level on the right in frames 4 and 5. In the foreground within arm's reach (0.4 to 1.0 m, brightest white), a rectangular tub on the bottom-left and a round mortar bucket at the bottom-centre sit about 0.3 m apart and partly occlude the floor behind them, while the camera wearer's right hand and forearm appear at the bottom-right in frame 3 at roughly 0.5 m depth to reach a trowel resting on a sack 1.0 to 1.3 m ahead. About 0.5 m to the right of the sack, a shallow round basin and a leaning wooden pole sit 1.5 to 1.8 m away at the base of the pillar, while in frame 5 a standing person on the lower exterior ground to the right of the pillar is rendered at roughly 2.0 to 2.5 m distance (about 1.2 m right of the basin and below the camera wearer's ledge), facing left toward the wall with their head and back partly cropped at the right frame boundary and out of everyone's arm's reach. Across the 5 frames, the depth gradient shifts leftward as the camera wearer turns clockwise from the dark interior sand pile toward the bright right-hand pillar and exterior drop-off. Compared to the high-contrast RGB strip where harsh sunlight and deep shadows obscure geometry, the depth map clearly separates the foreground sack, buckets, and dark interior wall plane, though it is unreliable along the thin wooden pole in frames 4 and 5 (where a web-like depth halo bleeds into the background wall) and flattens smaller tools like the wooden floats and trowels into the surfaces beneath them.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map is almost entirely black and fails to capture the scene layout, floor planes, walls, and most construction materials across the 5 frames as the camera wearer turns clockwise from the interior floor toward the right-hand exterior edge. It detects only a few isolated regions: a scoop on the back-left sand pile (2.5 m away) mislabelled as a 'boat' in frame 1, the camera wearer's reaching right forearm and hand at the bottom-centre of frame 3 (0.5 m away, within arm's reach of the foreground tools) labelled as 'person', the round metal basin at 1.5 to 1.8 m in front-right labelled as 'bowl' (with an overlapping 'fork' label in frame 4), a foreground trowel at 0.8 m below-left of the basin in frame 5 mislabelled as 'spoon', and an unlabelled pink strip along the right ledge edge in frame 4. In frame 5, it segments the person standing below and to the right of the ledge (2.0 to 2.5 m from the camera wearer and roughly 1.2 m right of the basin/bowl), whose silhouette faces left toward the building with their upper head and back partly out of view at the right border and no objects segmented within their arm's reach. As the camera pans right from frame 1 to frame 5, earlier detections on the left exit the view while the basin shifts from the right edge toward the centre-left and the standing person enters on the far right. While the clean silhouettes in frames 3 and 5 help isolate the boundary of the wearer's reaching arm and the standing person against cluttered, shadowed RGB backgrounds, the map is highly unreliable because it misses major foreground obstacles (the buckets at 0.5 to 0.8 m, the cement sack at 1.2 m, the concrete pillar, and the person's feet in frame 4) and assigns incorrect household categories to construction tools.
descriptions.pose: The pose map is completely blank (solid black) across all 5 frames, providing no spatial information about the scene layout, surfaces, or object distances as the camera wearer turns from left to right. It fails to detect the camera wearer's own right hand and forearm entering the bottom-centre foreground at about 0.5 m distance (within arm's reach of the trowel and sack at 1.0 to 1.3 m) in frame 3. It also misses the second person's lower legs and feet partly visible at the bottom-right corner in frame 4 (about 2.2 m away on the lower ground) as well as their nearly full standing body on the right in frame 5 (2.0 to 2.5 m from the camera wearer and 1.2 m right of the floor basin, standing below the ledge level). Consequently, the pose map cannot show that the person in frame 5 has their torso and head oriented leftward toward the building wall and slightly upward toward the camera wearer's vantage point, with their left hand held near their waist and their back partly cropped by the right frame edge. Unlike the RGB image—which clearly reveals the reaching egocentric hand in frame 3 and the standing person's body posture and head orientation in frame 5—the pose map offers no visibility advantages and is entirely unreliable throughout the sequence.
